transcript.answer: Otto uses one server-held TMS API key because the delivered OLT TMS API supports nothing else. It authenticates with a single global `x-api-key` header. It has no user login, no login endpoint, and no per-user credential. ADR-001 rejects Option A, where each user presents their own TMS credential and Otto forwards it. A user credential to forward doesn't exist, so customers can't present one. The ADR's context section (as retrieved) and the spec's Problem Statement say the same about Option B, where re:cinq would exchange or hold a user credential: there is nothing to exchange. Option C, a server-held key with the customer boundary enforced in Otto's own code, is the only option the published API supports. The TMS key is company-scoped, not user-scoped, so it can't narrow results by user role. Otto therefore enforces the rule that customers can only see their own bookings itself. Clerk authenticates the user, and the Clerk organisation carries the TMS `customerNumber`. A scope resolver in `apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts` derives that `customerNumber` from the authenticated company, never from the model or the request. Every TMS tool also runs an `ownership` check.

judgements.reason: The answer correctly says Otto holds one global key and enforces the customer boundary itself because the TMS has no user-level auth to forward. It omits the second essential reason, that the TMS issues one key per integration partner, which makes per-user credentials moot.
